en: Marcela Agoncillo and her daughter sewed the first Philippine flag in Hong Kong before it was officially unfurled in Kawit.
The Philippine eagle, our national bird, was originally called the monkey-eating eagle because locals believed it only ate monkeys.
Filipina pediatrician Fe del Mundo was the first woman ever admitted to Harvard Medical School, beating out all male applicants.
President Ramon Magsaysay popularized wearing the Barong Tagalog untucked outside his pants to prove he was not hiding a weapon.
T'boli women in South Cotabato create intricate T'nalak cloth from abaca fibers based on patterns revealed to them in dreams.
The ancient Baybayin writing system used by early Filipinos had only three vowels and fourteen consonants, written on bamboo and leaves.
National hero Jose Rizal sent a three-leaf clover to his family to symbolize his hope for their reunion before his execution.
The Ati-Atihan festival in Kalibo, Aklan, is considered the mother of all Philippine festivals and honors the Santo Niño.
Julian Felipe composed the Lupang Hinirang instrumental march in just three days, originally naming it Marcha Nacional Filipina.
Andres Bonifacio wrote the poem Pag-ibig sa Tinubuang Lupa, which translates to Love for the Native Land, while hiding from Spanish authorities.
Filipino painter Juan Luna won a gold medal at the 1884 Madrid Exposition of Fine Arts for his massive Spoliarium painting.
Spain sold the Philippines to the United States for twenty million dollars in the 1898 Treaty of Paris, ignoring Filipino independence.
